With him, from left: moderator Jesús Portillo García-Pintos, Andalusian mines director; Fernando Díaz Riopa, Touro/Atalaya Mining; Juan García Valledor, Pan Global Resources; and Juan Ignacio Artieda González Granda, Spain’s mining engineers’ council. Credit: C. McClelland
By: Colin McClelland in Seville October 21, 2026
Financing Spain’s next mines depends on giving investors credible development schedules, yet uncertain approvals make it difficult to plan major spending, developers told the Mining and Minerals Hall conference.
The challenge extends to Touro in Galicia, where a proposed copper operation backed by Atalaya Mining (LSE: ATYM) remains in permitting. A 2018 prefeasibility study envisaged annual production of about 30,000 tonnes over 12 years.
“You even have equipment that needs a year for manufacture and installation at the mine, and much more,” Fernando Díaz Riopa, general manager of Cobre San Rafael’s Touro project, said. “Every year we’re dealing with the problem of timelines.”
Wednesday’s panel, “Why projects fail to reach operation”, examined the gap between Spain’s mineral potential and the mines it can actually build. Companies must keep financing and fieldwork moving through years of approvals, while securing local support and the workers needed to turn technically viable deposits into operating mines, speakers said.
The sixth edition of the three-day conference runs through Thursday at Seville’s Fibes centre, bringing together 332 exhibitors. Organized by Spanish metallic mining association Aminer and promoted by Andalusia’s regional government, it focuses on mining’s role in Europe’s future.
The panel discussion followed Tuesday’s call by former Spanish foreign minister Ana Palacio for Europe to match U.S. mining support with stable policies, public investment and purchase guarantees.
Planning ahead
Developers need enough certainty to coordinate investment, equipment orders and recruitment, Díaz Riopa said. That requires working with authorities to establish realistic approval schedules.
Atalaya holds a 10% interest in Cobre San Rafael, which owns Touro, with the right to increase its stake to 80% as development milestones are met.
Infrastructure can also shape development costs. Díaz Riopa contrasted projects near Seville’s existing services with his experience in Mauritania, where securing water, power, port access and workers posed additional challenges.
Atalaya is already operating a water treatment plant at Touro to address acid runoff from the historical mine. The company brought that work forward ahead of a new environmental impact assessment to demonstrate how modern systems could remedy the damage.
Touro remains in permitting despite receiving strategic industrial status from Galicia’s government in June 2024, a designation intended to simplify procedures and shorten approval timelines.
Community share
At Touro, a social plan aims to deliver economic and social benefits to neighbours, Díaz Riopa said. The company works closely with local mayors.
“They have to feel that the mine is theirs,” Díaz Riopa said. “Not that a company arrives, extracts the minerals and the benefits leave. They have to feel that it’s part of them, that they participate, that they have a say, that their opinions count.”
Juan Ignacio Artieda González Granda, representing Spain’s mining engineers’ council, argued that distrust among residents, authorities and financiers underlies many development hurdles.
He proposed revising the surface-area-based mining levy so payments better reflect the value of the minerals extracted and flow to surrounding communities.
“They would have a right to a steady income throughout the life of the mine and wouldn’t have to live off the charity of the company operating there,” Artieda said.
Artieda also proposed independent technical reviews by qualified professionals to give authorities greater confidence in development applications and help accelerate approvals.
Jesús Portillo García-Pintos, the Andalusian government’s director general of mines and the panel moderator, pointed to Aznalcóllar as an example of linking investment to restoration. The region made responsibility for historical environmental liabilities a condition of awarding mining rights, he said.
Artieda pointed to the strain mining can place on local roads and bridges as a reason to give communities an assured financial return.
“We all like to have rights, not to be given charity,” he said.
Funding, workers
For explorers, delays can interrupt the fieldwork needed to keep investors engaged, Juan García Valledor, general manager for Spain at Pan Global Resources (TSXV: PGZ; US-OTC: PGZFF), said.
“A junior company dedicated exclusively to exploration needs continuous financing, which is not at all easy to obtain,” he said. “The money coming in has to be spent in a sustained way that meets what the investor demands.”
García Valledor also called for inactive mining rights to be released for fresh exploration. Andalusia is already courting investors with faster approvals and access to hundreds of areas covered by expired rights.
Spain’s exploration effort benefits from thousands of years of mining and nationwide geological mapping at a scale of 1:50,000, Manuel Regueiro y González-Barros of Spain’s scientific research council, CSIC, said. Staffing presents a different challenge.
“There aren’t enough technical personnel to take on these new and necessary jobs,” he said.

By Gavin van Marle

Australian infrastructure fund IFM Investors is set to acquire a 68% stake in Associated British Ports (ABP), following months of rumours about possible bidders circling the UK’s largest port owner and operator.
ABP shareholders Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and OMERS today said they agreed to terms with IFM Investors to sell each of their respective 33.9% and 30.0% stakes in ABP, which were originally acquired in 2015 and 2006 respectively.
The price tag was not disclosed, although The Financial Times estimated it to be over £10bn, with the deal seeing IFM shrug off competition from India’s Adani Group, as well as financial investors including Apollo and KKR.
However, it would appear the terms were sweet enough to convince CPP that its 10-year investment cycle in ABP had come to an end.
“This transaction represents an attractive opportunity to realize the value of our long-term investment and recycle capital into new opportunities, helping us deliver strong long-term returns for CPP contributors and beneficiaries, said James Bryce, managing director, Head of Infrastructure, CPP Investments.
According to the CapitalIQ platform, at the end of 2025 ABP boasted revenues of £792.5m and generated a net profit of £393.3m
“As an investor owned by Australian and UK pension funds, this transaction reflects our longstanding commitment to mobilising pension capital into UK infrastructure,” Kyle Mangini, Global Head of Infrastructure, IFM Investors, said.
“We look forward to supporting continued development of ABP’s infrastructure and operations, drawing on IFM’s long-term investment approach and experience across ports and other essential infrastructure assets,” he added.
Meanwhile, it is understood that existing minority shareholders such as Singapore sovereign wealth fund GIC and Kuwait’s Wren House will retain their holdings.
“Attracting investment from a fund managed by IFM Investors is a powerful endorsement of our business, our people and our strategy,” ABP chief executive Henrik Pedersen said.
“We are excited to unlock further growth opportunities, together with IFM Investors and our other shareholders, continuing ABP’s long-term investment benefitting our customers, our local communities, and the UK.”
The deal is expected to close in mid-2027.

source_document.body:
Phillips Connect launched two smart trailer products Sunday at the American Trucking Associations ’ Management Conference & Exhibition in Charlotte, North Carolina. Insights reads trailer sensor data to diagnose tire and lighting problems. TrailerSignal, a light on the trailer nose, shows green when a trailer is ready to dispatch and amber when it isn’t.
Both target defects that can slip past a walkaround and surface at a roadside inspection. Tire and lighting violations also count against a carrier’s Vehicle Maintenance BASIC under the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration ’s Compliance, Safety, Accountability program.
In the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance’s 2026 International Roadcheck , tires accounted for 2,914 of the 13,924 vehicle out-of-service violations, or 20.9%. Only brake systems produced more. Lights accounted for 1,659, or 11.9%.
“We help you answer those simple questions: are my lights working or are they at risk of failing?” Mark Wallin, president and general manager of Phillips Connect, told FreightWaves.
How fleets catch light and tire defects now
Federal rules require a driver to be satisfied that a truck’s lighting devices and tires are in good working order before driving. Every required lamp must be capable of being operated at all times .
Fleets “rely heavily today on a group of people in the yard to detect issues with a trailer’s lights,” Wallin said. Phillips Connect sensors already reported tire and light health data before Insights.
“Knowing that there’s something unusual on a circuit was the first step. With Insights, we can tell a fleet which circuit has the problem, what’s likely causing it, and what the technician should check,” he said.
Lights Insights names the faulty circuit
Phillips Connect Insights now names the faulty circuit, whether taillights, running lights, or marker lights, and separates partial faults from full ones, according to the company. It suggests a likely cause, such as a burned-out bulb or water in the lamp, and confirms when the fault clears.
Some faults come and go. Wallin described a situation where “a lamp might have a loose wire or water in a bulb, so it doesn’t work when you pick up the trailer in the morning, but as the day heats up the water evaporates and the light works again. Insights catches that pattern, so the technician knows there’s a real problem even when the light looks fine.”
Tire Insights looks for slow leaks
On tires, Insights flags slow leaks and shows which tire is losing air and how fast, even when pressure reads normal or the trailer runs an automatic tire inflation system (ATIS). It also flags ATIS malfunctions, pressure imbalance between paired tires, and miles driven on underinflated tires.
Wallin estimated that “maybe half” of trailers in the market are starting to come with ATIS, and that the systems give some fleets false confidence.
“Fleets running ATIS have made a smart investment in keeping their tires inflated. Insights shows them what that system is compensating for, so a slow leak gets fixed in the shop instead of growing into something worse – like a blowout – is avoided down the road,” he said.
Insights sends issues to fleet, safety, and maintenance teams in the Connect1 platform, urgent tire alerts to drivers through Phillips Connect’s DriverAssist, and diagnostics to technicians through the TechAssist app. It can also open service tickets in a fleet’s maintenance system.
TrailerSignal puts status on the trailer
TrailerSignal gives hostlers, dock crews, technicians, and drivers the same ready-or-not answer with no login or phone, according to the company.
“There are a lot of people in the yard who aren’t looking at a computer or a device, or this information isn’t available in a hostler system, or to your yard check person yet,” Wallin said.
The company rates the light as readable from 50 feet. A solar panel charges a built-in battery, so it works when the trailer is unplugged. It stays lit while the trailer is parked and shuts off once it moves. Installation takes as little as five minutes with no wiring.
Fleets choose which door, tire, light, and liftgate signals turn the light amber. One customer uses it at the dock, where amber tells a driver the trailer doors are still open.
“It can be a very dangerous, high-risk situation if that trailer is pulled away [while] the doors open,” Wallin said.
But the light only knows what the trailer’s sensors know. A fleet running any smart trailer sensor, including liftgate battery, tire, brakes, or more gets a red or amber signal on the nose of the trailer, Wallin said.
Neither release lists pricing, but the TrailerSignal and Insights are available now.
Phillips Connect adds to its trailer platform
The launches follow Phillips Connect’s March expansion into richer brake and liftgate data. The Irvine, California-based company named Wallin president and general manager in May. It plans to extend Insights to cargo activity during loading, unloading, and transit.
Wallin said the two products meet in the shop.
“Our mechanic finds the amber tag, pulls up our app, looks at the health of that trailer, and can find a slow leak,” he said. “Never could have had access to that kind of trailer data before.”
Why it matters: Tires and lights drove nearly a third of vehicle out-of-service violations in this year’s Roadcheck. Phillips Connect is putting its sensor data in front of yard crews, drivers, and technicians to catch those defects before an inspector does. Pricing has not been disclosed.
